## Design

### 2026-11-08: Spent 2 hours researching the problem of floating plastic pollution in lakes and understanding the challenges involved in keeping water surfaces clean.

**2h**

Spent 2 hours researching the problem of floating plastic pollution in lakes and understanding the challenges involved in keeping water surfaces clean.

I explored how plastic bottles, wrappers and other floating waste accumulate across water bodies, how wind and water currents can move waste to different locations, and why manual collection can become difficult when waste is spread across a large area.

Based on this research, I identified three main areas where AquaSwarm could potentially help: monitoring floating waste using an onboard camera, navigating across the water using a remotely controlled floating platform, and exploring a mechanism for collecting the waste.

I also began establishing the initial technical direction for the project, considering a twin-hull floating platform with a Raspberry Pi 4 for processing, an Arduino for motor control, a camera for monitoring and a Wi-Fi-based control system.

Outcome: Established the problem statement, identified the primary functions of AquaSwarm and outlined the initial technical direction for V0.1.

### 2026-11-08: Spent 2 hours developing the core concept and defining the objectives of AquaSwarm V0.1.

**2h**

Spent 2 hours developing the core concept and defining the objectives of AquaSwarm V0.1.

After identifying the problem of floating plastic pollution, I worked on converting the initial idea into a more structured engineering project. I established the main purpose of AquaSwarm as a remotely controlled floating robotic platform that can monitor water surfaces and help collect floating plastic waste.

I defined the primary subsystems, including the twin-hull floating platform, propulsion system, Raspberry Pi 4-based processing unit, Arduino-based motor control, onboard camera and Wi-Fi communication.

I also outlined the proposed operating sequence, from deploying the robot and establishing a wireless connection to monitoring the surroundings, navigating towards floating waste and collecting it.

An important part of this stage was separating the achievable features of V0.1 from the long-term vision. Features such as AI-based waste detection, GPS navigation and multi-robot coordination have been identified as future development goals rather than immediate requirements.

Outcome: Established the core project concept, primary objectives, proposed operating sequence, V0.1 scope and long-term development roadmap.

### 2026-11-08: Spent 2 hours developing the preliminary system architecture for AquaSwarm V0.1.

**2h**

Spent 2 hours developing the preliminary system architecture for AquaSwarm V0.1.

The main objective was to establish how the different electronic and mechanical subsystems would communicate and work together. I decided on a two-controller architecture using a Raspberry Pi 4 as the main processing unit and an Arduino as the dedicated motor controller.

I outlined the responsibilities of each controller, with the Raspberry Pi handling high-level processing, camera monitoring, wireless communication and the operator interface, while the Arduino would receive movement commands and manage the propulsion system through a suitable motor driver.

I also mapped out the proposed communication flow, starting from the operator sending commands over Wi-Fi to the Raspberry Pi, which would then communicate with the Arduino. The camera system would provide a live view of the surroundings through the monitoring interface.

Additionally, I explored the power distribution requirements, electronics protection, communication reliability and the need to separate motor power from sensitive computing electronics.

A preliminary system block diagram was created to represent the relationship between the controllers, camera, propulsion system, operator interface and power supply.

Outcome: Established the preliminary hardware architecture, controller responsibilities, communication flow and major subsystem connections for AquaSwarm V0.1.

### 2026-11-08: Spent 2 hours researching and defining the controller architecture for AquaSwarm V0.1.

**2h**

Spent 2 hours researching and defining the controller architecture for AquaSwarm V0.1.

I focused on selecting the responsibilities of the two main processing boards and understanding how they could work together efficiently.

The Raspberry Pi 4 was selected as the proposed main computing unit. Its responsibilities will include camera processing, wireless communication, hosting the remote-control interface, monitoring the robot and managing high-level system operations.

For hardware-level control, I decided to use an Arduino Uno. It will receive movement instructions from the Raspberry Pi and control the left and right propulsion motors through a suitable motor driver. This separation will allow the main computer to focus on processing while the microcontroller handles hardware operations.

I also explored UART serial communication as the proposed connection between the two boards. This would allow the Raspberry Pi to send movement commands to the Arduino and receive hardware status information in return.

Additionally, I identified important electrical considerations, including the difference between 3.3 V and 5 V logic levels, regulated power requirements, motor-driver compatibility and communication-loss protection.

Outcome: Established the proposed responsibilities of both controllers, selected UART as the communication method and defined the basic electronics architecture for AquaSwarm V0.1.

### 2026-11-08: iSpent 2 hours researching and evaluating possible propulsion systems for AquaSwarm V0.1.

**2h**

iSpent 2 hours researching and evaluating possible propulsion systems for AquaSwarm V0.1.

The main focus was understanding how a compact floating robot could move through water while maintaining effective steering and stability. I explored different propulsion approaches, including waterproof DC motors with propellers, brushless underwater thrusters and conventional motor-and-rudder arrangements.

After comparing their complexity, cost, waterproofing requirements and suitability for a small prototype, I established a preliminary preference for a twin-motor propulsion arrangement.

I also researched differential thrust, where the speed and direction of two independently controlled motors are varied to move and steer the robot. This approach could eliminate the need for a separate rudder and simplify the mechanical design.

The proposed control architecture uses the Arduino to manage the propulsion units through suitable motor drivers or electronic speed controllers, depending on the final motor selection.

Additionally, I identified important design considerations such as thrust requirements, power consumption, motor placement, propeller protection, waterproofing and communication-loss safety.

Outcome: Established the preliminary twin-motor differential-thrust propulsion concept, compared three propulsion approaches and identified the technical requirements for selecting the final motors and controllers.

### 2026-11-08: Spent 2 hours researching the floating platform and hull configuration for AquaSwarm V0.1.

**2h**

Spent 2 hours researching the floating platform and hull configuration for AquaSwarm V0.1.

The main objective was to identify a suitable structure that could support the electronic components, propulsion system, camera and proposed waste-collection mechanism while remaining stable on water.

I compared three different floating-platform configurations: monohull, catamaran and trimaran designs. After considering their structural complexity, available mounting space and potential stability, I identified the catamaran configuration as the preferred starting point for AquaSwarm.

I also explored the principles of buoyancy and displacement using Archimedes' principle, understanding how the combined weight of the robot determines the amount of water that must be displaced. Other factors studied included hull spacing, centre of gravity, weight distribution, freeboard and reserve buoyancy.

Based on this research, I developed a preliminary component arrangement with two parallel floating hulls, a central electronics platform, a front section reserved for waste collection, an elevated camera mount and rear-mounted propulsion units.

Additionally, I compared potential construction materials such as HDPE, PVC, marine plywood, closed-cell foam and 3D-printed plastics, considering their weight, durability, water resistance and fabrication requirements.

Outcome: Identified the catamaran as the preferred V0.1 hull configuration, established the preliminary component layout and researched the fundamental buoyancy and stability requirements for the floating platform.

### 2026-11-08: Spent 2 hours researching the camera and live monitoring subsystem for AquaSwarm V0.1.

**2h**

Spent 2 hours researching the camera and live monitoring subsystem for AquaSwarm V0.1.

Since the robot will operate remotely on water, I wanted to establish a reliable way for the operator to observe its surroundings and monitor its movement through a live video feed.

I explored different camera options compatible with the Raspberry Pi 4, including dedicated Raspberry Pi camera modules and USB webcams. I compared their integration requirements, size, connectivity and suitability for a compact floating robot.

I also developed the proposed video-streaming architecture, where the camera captures footage, the Raspberry Pi processes and streams it over a local Wi-Fi connection, and the operator views the feed through a browser-based monitoring dashboard. MJPEG over HTTP was identified as a possible initial streaming method.

Additionally, I outlined the proposed dashboard features, including a live camera window, connection indicators, camera status, battery information, movement controls and basic system telemetry.

I researched the factors affecting streaming performance, such as resolution, frame rate, bitrate, latency, wireless signal strength and processing load. I also considered camera placement, protective enclosures and the need to keep the camera above the expected waterline.

Finally, I explored future possibilities such as AI-based floating-waste detection, object classification and visual mapping, while keeping these features outside the immediate V0.1 scope.

Outcome: Established the proposed camera architecture, compared camera hardware options, identified a suitable direction for local video streaming and outlined the initial remote-monitoring dashboard.

### 2026-11-08: Spent 2 hours researching possible waste collection mechanisms for AquaSwarm V0.1.

**2h**

Spent 2 hours researching possible waste collection mechanisms for AquaSwarm V0.1.

The main objective was to determine how the robot could physically collect floating plastic waste while maintaining its stability and keeping the mechanical design relatively simple.

I explored three different approaches: a front-mounted mesh collection net, a motorised conveyor-based collection system and a guided collection basket. I compared these mechanisms based on their mechanical complexity, power requirements, maintenance, collection capacity and suitability for a small floating prototype.

After evaluating the alternatives, I identified a front-mounted mesh collection system with side guides as the preferred starting concept for V0.1. This arrangement could be positioned between the two hulls, allowing floating debris to enter the collection area while water drains through the mesh.

I also explored the proposed mechanical arrangement, including the collection opening, mesh platform, storage compartment and removable attachment. Particular attention was given to collection capacity, water drainage, additional weight and the effect of accumulated waste on the robot's buoyancy and stability.

Additionally, I considered possible future improvements such as motorised conveyors, automated waste transfer and AI-assisted waste identification, while keeping these outside the initial prototype requirements.

Outcome: Identified the preliminary front-mounted mesh collection concept, compared alternative collection mechanisms and established the main mechanical and operational requirements for AquaSwarm V0.1.

### 2026-11-08: Spent 2 hours researching the power system requirements for AquaSwarm V0.1.

**2h**

Spent 2 hours researching the power system requirements for AquaSwarm V0.1.

The main objective was to understand how the Raspberry Pi 4, Arduino, camera and propulsion motors would be powered while maintaining reliable operation on a portable floating platform.

I compared different power-source options, including USB power banks, protected rechargeable battery packs and RC battery systems. I explored their advantages, limitations and suitability for different sections of the robot.

I also researched the fundamentals of electrical power, voltage, current and battery capacity, using the relationships P = V × I and E = V × Ah to understand how the power requirements and potential operating duration could be estimated.

An important design decision was to separate the power paths for the computing electronics and propulsion system. The Raspberry Pi requires a stable regulated supply, whereas the motors can introduce sudden current demands that may affect sensitive electronics if the power system is not designed appropriately.

I developed a preliminary power-distribution architecture with a regulated electronics supply for the Raspberry Pi, Arduino and camera, alongside a suitable motor power path through the motor driver or ESCs.

Additionally, I identified requirements for battery protection, charging compatibility, voltage regulation, overcurrent protection, power switching, battery monitoring and waterproofing.

Outcome: Established the preliminary power-distribution architecture, compared portable power-source options and identified the electrical requirements that must be considered before selecting the final battery and power-management components.

### 2026-11-08: Spent 2 hours researching the communication and remote-control architecture for AquaSwarm V0.1.

**2h**

Spent 2 hours researching the communication and remote-control architecture for AquaSwarm V0.1.

The main objective was to establish how an operator could remotely control the robot, receive live camera footage and monitor its system status through a single interface.

I compared Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and dedicated radio-control communication methods. After considering their range, capabilities, hardware requirements and suitability for video transmission, I identified Wi-Fi as the preferred primary communication method for V0.1.

I developed a preliminary architecture in which the Raspberry Pi 4 acts as the central communication hub. It will receive commands from a phone or laptop through a browser-based dashboard, process them and forward movement instructions to the Arduino through UART serial communication.

I also researched possible software communication protocols, including HTTP for dashboard access and commands, WebSocket for real-time updates, MJPEG over HTTP for camera streaming and JSON for exchanging structured movement and status information.

Another important part of this stage was planning offline operation. I explored configuring the Raspberry Pi as a local Wi-Fi access point, allowing the operator to connect directly to AquaSwarm without requiring an external internet connection.

Finally, I identified communication reliability requirements, including connection monitoring, command validation, motor shutdown after communication loss and an emergency-stop function.

Outcome: Established the proposed Wi-Fi-based communication architecture, identified the software protocols for remote control and monitoring, and outlined the requirements for reliable offline operation.

### 2026-11-08: Spent 2 hours evaluating the technical feasibility of AquaSwarm V0.1 and consolidating the research completed during the previous development stages.

**2h**

Spent 2 hours evaluating the technical feasibility of AquaSwarm V0.1 and consolidating the research completed during the previous development stages.

I reviewed the complete proposed architecture, covering the twin-hull floating platform, Raspberry Pi 4, Arduino, propulsion system, camera, wireless communication and front-mounted waste collection mechanism.

I assessed each subsystem based on its implementation complexity, technical requirements and potential challenges. Particular attention was given to buoyancy, platform stability, waterproofing, power consumption, wireless connectivity, propulsion efficiency and collection capacity.

I also conducted a preliminary risk analysis, identifying possible issues such as water entering the electronics enclosure, insufficient buoyancy, battery depletion, motor overheating, wireless disconnection and collection-system overload. Possible mitigation approaches were outlined for each of these risks.

Another important part of this stage was preparing the preliminary Bill of Materials. I listed the major electronic, mechanical and electrical components required for the prototype, including the Raspberry Pi 4, Arduino Uno, camera, propulsion units, motor drivers, rechargeable power system, floating hull materials and collection mechanism.

I also developed an initial budget estimate of approximately $140 to $240, covering the major prototype components and supporting materials. This estimate will be refined once the exact hardware specifications and suppliers are finalised. However, I already have a Raspberry Pi 4, so the price will be reducing greatly.

Finally, I established a preliminary development priority list to guide the transition from research and planning towards actual hardware integration and testing.

Outcome: Completed the initial technical feasibility assessment, identified major engineering risks and their proposed mitigation strategies, prepared the preliminary Bill of Materials and established an estimated prototype budget and development priorities.
